Classic Hodgkin lymphoma mainly involves lymph nodes, with a striking preference for nodes above the diaphragm: more than 70 percent of patients with early-stage disease present with enlarged cervical or supraclavicular nodes, more than 60 percent have mediastinal involvement, and fewer than 5 percent have disease only below the diaphragm. The nodes are painless and firm, and the disease involves contiguous node groups, one to the next. Disease starting outside the nodes (skin, GI tract, Waldeyer ring, CNS) is rare. B symptoms appear in about 20 percent of localized and 70 percent of advanced disease. A rare but distinctive symptom: pain in the affected nodes after drinking alcohol. 4 AML's diagnostic threshold (20 percent blasts for most AML, any count with a defining genetic abnormality), blasts and Auer rods (which exclude ALL), AML versus ALL, and the conditions it can grow out of (myelodysplastic syndrome) Study guide + objectives · 6 questions in the bank The number his objectives ask for is the blast threshold. For the AML types defined by a genetic abnormality, "you can diagnose AML no matter blast count". For the others, the blasts must be over 20 percent, the threshold his objectives call the one for diagnosing most AML. Fewer blasts than that, in a patient with abnormal counts, point to something else, such as a myelodysplastic syndrome (later in these notes). Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): persistent cytopenias with abnormal function and look of the red cell, granulocyte and/or megakaryocyte precursors. It may start with few blasts and progress to more. The myeloproliferative neoplasms, with persistently high counts: polycythemia vera (increased red cells), essential thrombocythemia (increased platelets) and primary myelofibrosis (fibrosis in the marrow). 5 ALL, the acute leukemia of young children: B-ALL most often, and T-ALL, told apart by markers rather than by looks Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank His acute column says "usually children and the young", but his AML slide gives AML a median age of 65 and calls it common in adults. Both hold: ALL is the acute leukemia of young children, and AML is the acute leukemia of older adults. If a question asks who gets AML, it is adults. 6 Chronic myeloid leukemia: BCR::ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, chronic versus blast phase, a leukocytosis of maturing neutrophils, imatinib Study guide + objectives · 4 questions in the bank Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (the slides join the two names with a double colon), with too many neutrophils, a neutrophilic granulocytosis. At diagnosis, 90 to 95 percent carry the reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22), which makes the shortened chromosome 22 called the Philadelphia chromosome. 7 CLL/SLL: soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells in the blood; one disease, split by a B-cell count of 5 × 10⁹/L; older patients; infections from too little antibody; largely incurable Study guide + objectives · 3 questions in the bank The look, which his objective stresses "particularly in blood": small lymphocytes with clumped chromatin, a pattern compared to cracked mud or a soccer ball, and many smudge cells, fragile lymphocytes crushed flat as the smear is made. In the marrow the involvement can be nodular, interstitial, diffuse, or a mix. In a lymph node the small cells infiltrate diffusely, with pale areas of larger cells called proliferation centers. 8 Burkitt lymphoma: endemic versus sporadic and their EBV rates, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky, the jaw; the other lymphomas tied to EBV Study guide + objectives · 4 questions in the bank Under the microscope: sheets of uniform, medium-sized, cohesive blue cells, with many tingible-body macrophages scattered among them. These macrophages have eaten the debris of tumor cells that died by apoptosis, and their pale cytoplasm against the dark blue sheet gives the classic starry-sky pattern. With modern immunochemotherapy including rituximab, in high-resource settings, the prognosis is excellent: overall survival over 90 percent in children and 80 percent in adults. 9 Mantle cell lymphoma: from the follicle's mantle zone, t(11;14) switching on cyclin D1, older adults with enlarged nodes, survival now longer than it was Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank Its genetic hallmark, and the first event in its development, is the translocation between chromosomes 11 and 14, t(11;14), present in at least 95 percent of cases. It switches on cyclin D1, and his slide calls the cyclin D1 stain diagnostic. 10 Mycosis fungoides (patches, then plaques, then tumors; epidermotropic T cells with cerebriform nuclei; indolent) and Sézary syndrome (erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy and Sézary cells in the blood; aggressive) Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank Know this From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Borak's lecture. Place the four leukemias on two axes (acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid) and know each one's look: AML's blasts and Auer rods, ALL in young children, CML's Philadelphia chromosome, CLL's smudge cells. Know the two ways leukemia does harm (marrow failure: anemia, bleeding, infection; infiltration: spleen, liver, nodes, bone, gums), Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin (Reed-Sternberg cells and contiguous nodes above the diaphragm, versus mostly B-cell and often extranodal), and the lymphomas by their associations: Burkitt (t(8;14), MYC, EBV, the jaw), mantle cell (t(11;14), cyclin D1), mycosis fungoides (patches, plaques, tumors) and Sézary syndrome (erythroderma, nodes, Sézary cells in the blood). Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin; with Sézary syndrome it is the most common type of cutaneous lymphoma, more than half of cases. Its lesions evolve in sequence: patches, then plaques, then tumors. They can be one or many; when localized they favor sun-protected skin, the flexures (armpits and groin) and the lower trunk and buttocks, a "bathing-trunk" distribution. Under the microscope, small to medium-sized T cells with a clear halo and hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted ("cerebriform") nuclei line up along the basal layer and infiltrate the epidermis: they are epidermotropic. The course is indolent, over years or decades, with lesions that persist and grow slowly. It can appear at any age, peaking in the late fifties. Sézary syndrome is defined by a triad: erythroderma (red skin over most of the body), generalized lymphadenopathy, and clonal T cells with cerebriform nuclei, Sézary cells, in the skin, the lymph nodes and the peripheral blood. Unlike mycosis fungoides, it is aggressive: the 5-year survival is 10 to 30 percent, and most patients die of opportunistic infections. 11 The other B-cell lymphomas and their associations: follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) and BCL2, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (about 30 percent, de novo or transformed), and the infections behind MALT lymphoma Study guide + objectives · 8 questions in the bank The event that starts it is the translocation between chromosomes 14 and 18, t(14;18), found in 85 to 90 percent of cases. It moves the BCL2 gene next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene, IGH, so BCL2 is switched on all the time (his slide: "constitutive expression of BCL2"). BCL2 blocks apoptosis, so the cells live on instead of dying. The neoplastic follicles stain for BCL2, which helps separate them from reactive follicles. The retinoic acid lets the blocked promyelocytes mature. 13 The other T- and NK-cell lymphomas: peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS (aggressive), and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of the nose and palate Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is a lymphoma of NK-cell or T-cell lineage that damages and destroys blood vessels, with prominent necrosis, and a very strong association with EBV. It begins in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, Waldeyer ring or epiglottis. From the nose it can grow out into the face or erode the nasal floor, destroying and perforating the hard palate, the picture once called "lethal midline granuloma". A dentist may be the first to see it. 14 Diagnosing lymphoma: tissue sampling, a fresh specimen (not formalin) for flow cytometry, forward and side scatter, the B symptoms Objectives · 4 questions in the bank Unexplained weight loss of at least 10 percent of body weight over the past 6 months That is why the specimen handling matters. When you collect the specimen, don't put it in formalin: formalin fixes the cells, and flow cytometry needs them fresh. It may need a special medium, such as RPMI or Hanks's solution. 15 Plasma cell neoplasms: plasmacytoma versus multiple myeloma, rouleaux, the M-spike and CRAB Objectives · 3 questions in the bank Plasma cell myeloma is a bone marrow-based, multifocal proliferation of plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is plasma cell myeloma, usually with a monoclonal immunoglobulin in the serum or urine, plus either organ damage from the disease or, without it, lab or imaging findings that predict organ damage within 2 years. It is considered incurable for most patients. His slides show the findings: lytic bone lesions (punched-out holes in the bone on radiographs); an M-spike on protein electrophoresis, the monoclonal protein as one tall, narrow band; the CRAB features of organ damage, which stand for hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions; and rouleaux on the blood smear, red cells stacked like coins, because the large amount of immunoglobulin protein makes them stick together.
